source.title: Self-Regularity of Non-Negative Output Weights for Overparameterized Two-Layer Neural Networks
source.authors: D. Gamarnik; Eren C. Kızıldağ; Ilias Zadik

record.tranche_reason: The paper proves algorithm-independent generalization guarantees for shallow networks using outer-norm and fat-shattering bounds. This bears on the broad generalization claim, but it does not test the specific empirical conditions in V1–V8.
record.gate_note: The paper reports theoretical bounds, not experiments on natural or random labels. It does not test whether the listed architectures, optimizers, batch sizes, regularizers, or measured properties change the training–test gap.
record.test_reason: The study proves conditional population squared-error bounds for two-layer networks with non-negative output weights. None of its results tests V1–V8. In particular, a width-independent upper bound does not establish that widening lowers test error, and an outer-norm bound does not test magnitude-aware sharpness.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors establish algorithm-independent outer-norm bounds and derive population squared-error guarantees for two-layer networks with non-negative output weights under stated assumptions. ReLU and step outer norms use normalized internal weights. Generalization sample complexity is near-linear for step networks and sigmoid networks with polynomially bounded internal weights, and polynomial of higher degree for ReLU.
record.recipe_differences: Theoretical covering-number and fat-shattering analysis; no trained model or empirical training recipe is evaluated.
record.method_sensitivity: The guarantees depend on activation, non-negative output weights, distributional assumptions, and sample-size conditions; ReLU has an additional distributional condition and a different error bound.

fits_no_version.finding: Theorem 3.1 bounds population squared error uniformly over low-training-error sigmoid, ReLU, and step networks with non-negative output weights, subject to activation-specific assumptions. These are theoretical guarantees rather than observed performance comparisons.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under specified distributional and weight assumptions, low empirical squared error implies bounded population squared error for two-layer networks, with sufficient sample size independent of network width.

record.problems: The results are theoretical and conditional on non-negative output weights and distributional assumptions; they do not establish the empirical natural-label/random-label comparison or quantify observed test error. The ReLU bound includes an additional distributional requirement.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label versus random-label held-out accuracy under the same architecture and training recipe.
Whether increasing width beyond interpolation lowers test error; the bounds are uniform in width and establish no decreasing trend.
Convolutional versus fully connected image-classification performance and the role of local connectivity or initialization.
Held-out performance of adaptive optimizers versus SGD under different tuning or weight-decay recipes.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that reduce their penalty.
Dropout effects on held-out error across training-set sizes, dropout strengths, and augmentation regimes.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its correlation or ranking agreement with generalization gaps.
Test-accuracy effects of removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: Theoretical results can test a claim, but these theorems address a different proposition from V1–V8. The introduction's discussion of interpolation and improving accuracy with width cites prior work; it is not this study's own result.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label fitting or held-out accuracy comparison for the same architectures and recipes.
No width sweep or test-error trend past the interpolation threshold.
No comparison of convolutional and fully connected networks.
No sharpness or other generalization-measure comparison.
